orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint on the ground that their deposition transcripts were inadmissible.

facts.factual_summary: The decedent allegedly slipped in defendants’ Brooklyn building on June 2, 2012. No one witnessed the fall. Her husband described wet clothes and liquid smelling of Ajax on the steps and floor; her niece reported a dry floor and no problem with the steps.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants did not establish that they had not created the alleged condition.
Defendants failed to negate actual notice of the alleged condition.
The property manager described only general practices, with no evidence of when the specific area was last inspected or cleaned.
The conflicting accounts of conditions after the unwitnessed fall left a triable issue of causation. Defendants did not show the cause was unidentifiable.

The court accepted the husband’s, niece’s and manager’s unsigned transcripts and the responsive reply proof concerning the niece. The unsworn staff statements were inadmissible. Even with the transcripts, the defense failed its initial burden.

evidence_discussed.description: The husband’s deposition described the scene after he found the decedent.
The niece described a dry floor. The property manager described general practices; the superintendent’s and porter’s unsworn statements were rejected.
The verified bill of particulars attributed the fall to a slippery liquid.

quality.notes: The affirmance preserved the denial of dismissal on different grounds. The record does not establish that Ajax was present or that the fall caused the decedent’s later death.

evidence.quote: the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Dawn Jimenez-Salta, J.), dated October 25, 2017. The order denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
On June 2, 2012, the plaintiff's decedent allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell in a building located in Brooklyn that was owned and managed by the defendants.
There were no eyewitnesses to the decedent's fall, and she died in February 2015.
The Supreme Court denied the motion on the ground that the deposition transcripts submitted by the defendants in support of their motion were not in admissible evidentiary form.

Although the plaintiff's deposition transcript, which the defendants submitted in support of their motion, was unsigned, it was nonetheless admissible as the plaintiff raised no objection to its submission or accuracy and, in fact, requested that the Supreme Court "incorporate" his transcript into his opposition
the defendants demonstrated that they had submitted the unsigned transcript to the decedent's niece for review, but that she failed to sign and return it within 60 days.
the court should have considered it, because it was in direct response to allegations raised for the first time in the plaintiff's opposition papers
The unsigned deposition transcript of the defendants' property manager was admissible under CPLR 3116 (a) since it was submitted by the defendants themselves and thus adopted as accurate
we affirm, albeit on grounds different from those relied upon by the Supreme Court.
The plaintiff alleged, in his bill of particulars, inter alia, that the decedent slipped and fell on a "liquid slippery substance."
During his deposition, he testified that when he found the decedent lying on the floor, her clothes were wet and he observed liquid that smelled like "Ajax" on the steps and on the floor.
The decedent's niece testified at her deposition that upon finding her aunt on the floor, she did not see any issue with the steps and that the floor was not wet.

Since the plaintiff's deposition testimony and the decedent's niece's deposition testimony were in conflict, the defendants failed to eliminate all triable issues of fact as to the cause of the decedent's fall
The defendants also failed to establish, prima facie, that they did not create or have actual or constructive notice of the alleged dangerous condition on the step and floor where the decedent fell
The written statements of the building's superintendent and porter were both unsworn and not in admissible form
Moreover, the deposition testimony of the defendants' property manager referred to only general cleaning or inspection practices.
It was devoid of any evidence as to when, prior to the decedent's fall, the specific area where she fell was last cleaned or inspected
Since the defendants failed to demonstrate their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers need not be reviewed

orders.description: Westchester County order dated June 30, 2017, insofar as appealed from
orders.trial_court_action: Denied Edison’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint against it.

facts.factual_summary: Behluli allegedly slipped on an interior stair in a Manhattan hotel owned by Edison and leased to her employer. She alleged that cracked and missing vinyl exposed slippery metal underneath.

legal_issues.finding: Edison established that it had assumed no maintenance duty by contract or conduct. Its reentry right did not supply a basis for liability on this record.
The parties disputed constructive notice, but the appellate court expressly declined to reach it.
Edison established its out-of-possession defense, and Behluli did not raise a triable issue.
Even with a right of reentry, Edison showed the alleged condition was not a significant structural or design defect violating a specific statutory provision.

quality.notes: The court reversed the entire portion appealed by Edison and granted dismissal against Edison alone.

evidence.quote: the defendant Edison Management Company, LLC, appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Westchester County (Alan D. Scheinkman, J.), dated June 30, 2017. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied that defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

Ordered that the order is reversed insofar as appealed from, on the law, with costs, and the motion of the defendant Edison Management Company, LLC, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it is granted.

The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on an interior stairwell of a hotel in Manhattan, which was owned by the defendant Edison Management Company, LLC (hereinafter Edison), and leased to the plaintiff's employer.
The plaintiff alleged that the vinyl material covering the stair on which she slipped was cracked and missing, revealing the slippery, metallic stair underneath.
Here, Edison demonstrated, prima facie, that it was an out-of-possession landlord that did not assume a duty to maintain the premises by contract or by a course of conduct

although the plaintiff alleged the violation of a statutory duty, and Edison retained a right to reenter the premises for the purposes of inspection and repairs, Edison demonstrated, prima facie, that the alleged defect was not a significant structural or design defect in violation of a specific statutory provision
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted Edison's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.
we need not address the parties' remaining contentions regarding whether Edison had constructive notice of the condition.

orders.trial_court_action: Granted Colonial Woods’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Sullivan allegedly tripped on the driveway next to the concrete apron outside a condominium garage. Colonial Woods maintained the common-area driveway. The opinion gives no measurement or precise description of the defect.

legal_issues.finding: The trial court alternatively found no actual notice. The appellate court affirmed on triviality.
Lack of constructive notice was an alternative trial-court ground. The appellate holding rested on triviality.
The court considered the photographs and Sullivan’s account of the circumstances and found the alleged defect trivial. It did not rely on a numerical height threshold.

evidence_discussed.description: The defense submitted Sullivan’s deposition describing the time, place and circumstances.
The homeowners’ association president’s deposition was submitted.
The court relied particularly on photographs of the accident site.

quality.notes: The court did not adopt the alternative notice rationale as a separate basis for affirmance.

evidence.quote: the plaintiffs appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Thomas Whelan, J.), dated July 8, 2016. The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

On May 24, 2013, the plaintiff Nancy Sullivan (hereinafter the injured plaintiff) allegedly was injured when she tripped and fell on a portion of a driveway adjacent to a concrete apron located in front of a condominium unit garage at 2 Bartlett Commons in Yaphank.
The driveway was a common area and maintained by the defendant.

The Supreme Court granted the motion, finding that the alleged defect was trivial and therefore not actionable. Alternatively, the court also determined that the defendant had neither actual nor constructive notice of the alleged defect.
There is no "minimal dimension test" or "per se rule" that the condition must be of a certain height or depth in order to be actionable

Here, the defendant, in support of its motion for summary judgment, relied upon, inter alia, the injured plaintiff's deposition testimony, the deposition testimony of the president of the defendant's homeowners' association, and photographs of the accident site.

Considering the evidence presented, particularly the photographs and the plaintiff's description of the time, place, and circumstance of the injury, the defendant established, prima facie, that the alleged defect was trivial as a matter of law and, therefore, not actionable
In opposition, the plaintiffs failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination that the defendant was entitled to summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.trial_court_action: Granted the restaurant tenant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Shortly after midnight on January 29, 2017, Montalvo fell while stepping down from a strip mall walkway to its parking lot after leaving the restaurant. She testified that the area was dark because the restaurant’s exterior lights were off.

legal_issues.finding: The tenant did not own, occupy, control or specially use the common area. Neither the lease nor the limited requirement to illuminate signs and display windows created a duty to light the common area for third parties.

evidence_discussed.description: Montalvo testified about lighting at the accident site and elsewhere in the parking lot.
The lease governed lighting of signs and display windows during mall hours and did not require the tenant to illuminate the common areas.

quality.notes: The site is described as a strip-mall common area outside the restaurant tenant’s control. The court identifies a fall while stepping down but does not specify a slip, trip, or loss of footing. Retain for mechanism review; the affirmance is unambiguous.

evidence.quote: the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Thomas Feinman, J.), dated August 1, 2019. The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

Shortly after midnight on January 29, 2017, after exiting a restaurant owned by the defendant, which was located in a strip mall, the plaintiff fell as she attempted to step down from a walkway abutting the restaurant to the asphalt parking lot.

The plaintiff thereafter commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries against the defendant, a tenant of the strip mall, alleging that it breached a duty of care to keep the exterior lights of the restaurant turned on.

The plaintiff testified at her deposition that other lights in the parking lot were illuminated, but that it was dark in the area where the accident occurred because the restaurant's exterior lights had been turned off.
The defendant moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint on the ground that it had no duty to illuminate the common area where the accident occurred.
a tenant's common-law duty to maintain premises in a reasonably safe condition is limited to those areas which it occupies and controls, or makes a special use

Here, the defendant established, prima facie, that it did not own, occupy, control, or [*2] make special use of the common area where the incident occurred, and that it did not have a duty to illuminate the area
Moreover, the lease between the defendant and the landlord did not obligate the defendant to illuminate the common areas.

a lease provision obligating the defendant to keep its display windows and store front signage electrically lit only during the time that the strip mall was open did not create a duty owed to third parties such as the plaintiff
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to whether the defendant owed her a duty of care.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Suffolk County order dated February 2, 2010, as limited by the appellant’s brief
orders.trial_court_action: Denied the branch of defendants’ motion seeking summary judgment dismissing the complaint against Constantopoulos.

facts.factual_summary: Mignogna allegedly slipped on black ice in the parking lot of the 7-Eleven franchise owned by Constantopoulos. His employees were responsible for shoveling and salting the accident area.

legal_issues.finding: Constantopoulos failed to establish that he did not create the patch of ice.
He failed to establish lack of actual notice.
He offered no evidence from the employees on site about when the lot was last inspected, shoveled or plowed. Constructive notice remained disputed.
Because the appellant failed his initial burden, the court did not need to assess Mignogna’s opposition.

evidence_discussed.description: Evidence from the employees responsible for clearing the lot was missing on the timing of the last inspection or snow removal.

quality.notes: The source identifies the franchisee’s ownership of the store and employees’ maintenance of the lot. The appeal concerned dismissal only as against that appellant.

evidence.quote: the defendant Guy Constantopoulos appeals, as limited by his brief, from so much of an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Costello, J.), dated February 2, 2010, as denied that branch of the defendants’ motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him.
Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

This action arises from the plaintiffs alleged slip and fall on a patch of black ice in the parking lot of a 7-Eleven store, owned by the defendant Guy Constantopoulos (hereinafter the appellant) pursuant to a franchise agreement.

In moving for summary judgment, the appellant failed to establish, prima facie, that he did not create the icy condition that allegedly caused the plaintiff to slip and fall or that he lacked actual or constructive notice of it

In support of his motion, the appellant failed to submit evidence from his employees who were at the premises on the day of the accident and who were responsible for shoveling and salting the area where the plaintiff allegedly fell, stating when the parking lot was last inspected, shoveled, or plowed
Under these circumstances, it cannot be said, as a matter of law, that there was no triable issue of fact as to the appellant’s liability for causing the plaintiffs accident.
Since the appellant failed to meet his prima facie burden, it is not necessary to consider the sufficiency of the plaintiffs opposition papers
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied that branch of the defendants’ motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against the appellant
